title: Dermatologist-level classification of skin cancer with deep neural networks
author: Andre Esteva · Brett Kuprel · Roberto A. Novoa · Justin Ko · Susan M. Swetter · Helen M. Blau · Sebastian Thrun

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The supplied material is only a bibliography fragment concerning deep-learning methods and computer-aided skin-cancer diagnosis. It provides no substantive findings or argument about legal AI, task-level capability, verification, selective deployment, or legal-work redesign, so the source’s position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

mo.t: Clinical support: Practitioner gains may not help patients

kp.k: A single CNN achieved dermatologist-comparable image classification
kp.d: The authors report dermatologist-comparable performance on three image-based tasks: keratinocyte carcinoma classification, melanoma classification using standard photographs, and melanoma classification using dermoscopy. The same network performed all three tasks. These findings concern dermatology, not legal services, and comparisons were explicitly restricted to image classification.
qs: Using a single convolutional neural network trained on general skin lesion classification, we match the performance of at least 21 dermatologists tested across three critical diagnostic tasks: keratinocyte carcinoma classification, melanoma classification and melanoma classification using dermoscopy.
We restrict the comparisons to image-based classification.

kp.k: Large datasets and transfer learning supported automated classification
kp.d: The study used 129,450 clinical images covering 2,032 diseases, including 3,374 dermoscopy images. An Inception v3 CNN pretrained on approximately 1.28 million ImageNet images across 1,000 object categories was fine-tuned across all layers. The authors attribute robustness to photographic variability to the combined pretraining and dermatology data, rather than standardized imaging alone.
qs: We demonstrate generalizable classification with a new dermatologist-labelled dataset of 129,450 clinical images, including 3,374 dermoscopy images.

We utilize a GoogleNet Inception v3 CNN architecture9 that was pretrained on approximately 1.28 million images (1,000 object categories) from the 2014 ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge6, and train it on our dataset using transfer learning28.
We overcome this challenge by using a data-driven approach—1.41 million pre-training and training images make classification robust to photographic variability.

kp.k: End-to-end learning removed hand-crafted visual feature requirements
kp.d: Unlike earlier systems relying on extensive preprocessing, lesion segmentation and domain-specific feature extraction, the authors trained directly from pixels and disease labels, using one network for photographs and dermoscopy. Medical expertise still informed labels and the disease taxonomy.
qs: Many previous techniques require extensive preprocessing, lesion segmentation and extraction of domain-specific visual features before classification.
By contrast, our system requires no hand-crafted features; it is trained end-to-end directly from image labels and raw pixels, with a single network for both photographic and dermoscopic images.
The full taxonomy contains 2,032 diseases and is organized based on visual and clinical similarity of diseases.

kp.k: Expert taxonomy improved classification through finer training categories
kp.d: Dermatologists organized diseases by clinical and visual similarity; a recursive partitioning algorithm produced 757 training classes with maxClassSize = 1,000. Probabilities for broader inference categories were recovered by summing descendant training-class probabilities. Nine-fold cross-validation showed improvements from 69.4 ± 0.8% to 72.1 ± 0.9% for three-way classification and from 48.9 ± 1.9% to 55.4 ± 1.7% for nine-way classification compared with direct training on those broader classes.
qs: It was derived by dermatologists using a bottom-up procedure: individual diseases, initialized as leaf nodes, were merged based on clinical and visual similarity, until the entire structure was connected.
With maxClassSize = 1,000 this algorithm yields 757 training classes.
To recover the probability of any inference node we simply sum the probabilities of its descendant training nodes.

A CNN trained on a finer disease partition performs better than one trained directly on three or nine classes (see Extended Data Table 2), demonstrating the effectiveness of our partitioning algorithm.

kp.k: Broad diagnostic validation had weaker ground-truth evidence
kp.d: Three-way validation accuracy was 72.1 ± 0.9%, compared with 65.56% and 66.0% for two dermatologists; nine-way accuracy was 55.4 ± 1.7%, compared with 53.3% and 55.0%. The dermatologists assessed 180 images per task, while CNN results reflected nine-fold cross-validation. The authors explicitly describe these comparisons as inconclusive because labels were not necessarily biopsy-confirmed, treating them as evidence of relevant learning rather than definitive diagnostic validation.
qs: In this task, the CNN achieves 72.1 ± 0.9% (mean ± s.d.) overall accuracy (the average of individual inference class accuracies) and two dermatologists attain 65.56% and 66.0% accuracy on a subset of the validation set.
The CNN achieves 55.4 ± 1.7% overall accuracy whereas the same two dermatologists attain 53.3% and 55.0% accuracy.

Because images of the validation set are labelled by dermatologists, but not necessarily confirmed by biopsy, this metric is inconclusive, and instead shows that the CNN is learning relevant information.

kp.k: Biopsy-proven comparisons measured sensitivity and specificity
kp.d: Direct comparisons used 135 epidermal images, 130 melanocytic photographs and 111 melanocytic dermoscopy images, assessed by 25, 22 and 21 dermatologists respectively. Dermatologists chose biopsy/treatment or reassurance; the CNN generated malignancy probabilities, with thresholds swept to produce sensitivity–specificity curves. AUC exceeded 91% for each comparison. The authors report that most dermatologist operating points fell below the CNN curve; this is a threshold-dependent comparison, not a single reported accuracy percentage.
qs: For each image the dermatologists were asked whether to biopsy/treat the lesion or reassure the patient.
The CNN outperforms any dermatologist whose sensitivity and specificity point falls below the blue curve of the CNN, which most do.
The area under the curve (AUC) for each case is over 91%.
The images for this comparison (135 epidermal, 130 melanocytic and 111 melanocytic dermoscopy images) are sampled from the full test sets.

kp.k: Larger test sets yielded similar discrimination performance
kp.d: The complete biopsy-labelled evaluation comprised 707 epidermal images, 225 melanocytic photographs and 1,010 melanocytic dermoscopy images, totalling 1,942. AUC changes relative to the smaller expert-comparison samples were below 0.03. A separate dermatologist question—whether lesions appeared malignant or benign—also produced results described as on par with individual dermatologists and above their average.
qs: The sensitivity and specificity curves for our entire test set of biopsy-labelled images comprised 707 epidermal, 225 melanocytic and 1,010 melanocytic dermoscopy images (Fig. 3b).
We observed negligible changes in AUC (< 0.03) when we compared the sample dataset (Fig. 3a) with the full dataset (Fig. 3b), validating the reliability of our results on a larger dataset.
As in Fig. 3, the CNN is on par with the performance of the dermatologists and outperforms the average.

kp.k: Evaluation controlled overlap but selected higher-quality images
kp.d: The authors grouped related images to prevent training–validation leakage and report no lesion overlap between test and training/validation sets. Testing used independent, high-quality repositories with biopsy-proven images. Blurry and distant images were excluded from validation and testing, and a diagnosis-blinded dermatologist removed insufficient-resolution images from the direct-comparison samples. Binary inference also assumed the lesion was already known to be melanocytic or epidermal.
qs: Blurry images and far-away images were removed from the test and validation sets, but were still used in training.
No overlap (that is, same lesion, multiple viewpoints) exists between the test sets and the training/validation data.

However in the binary classification cases, the images in question are known to be either melanocytic or epidermal and so we utilize only the training classes that are descendants of either melanocytic or epidermal classes.

kp.k: Network and dermatologists shared important classification difficulties
kp.d: Nine-way confusion matrices showed similar mistakes by the CNN and two dermatologists, including confusion between benign and malignant melanocytic lesions, misclassification into the highly variable inflammatory category, and difficulty recognizing malignant dermal tumours. Internal-feature visualizations showed disease clustering, while saliency maps indicated attention to lesions rather than background or healthy skin.
qs: Classes 7 and 8—benign and malignant melanocytic lesions—are often confused with each other.
Many images are mistaken as class 6, the inflammatory class, owing to the high variability of diseases in this category.
These tumours are essentially nodules under the skin that are challenging to visually diagnose.
As can be seen, the network fixates most of its attention on the lesions themselves and ignores background and healthy skin.

kp.k: Clinical deployment required further real-world validation
kp.d: The authors explicitly distinguish isolated-image classification from full clinical diagnosis, which incorporates contextual information. They recommend evaluation in actual clinical settings across the full spectrum of lesions encountered in practice. Their findings therefore do not establish equivalent performance across an entire dermatologist’s role.
qs: Further research is necessary to evaluate performance in a real-world, clinical setting, in order to validate this technique across the full distribution and spectrum of lesions encountered in typical practice.

Whilst we acknowledge that a dermatologist’s clinical impression and diagnosis is based on contextual factors beyond visual and dermoscopic inspection of a lesion in isolation, the ability to classify skin lesion images with the accuracy of a board-certified dermatologist has the potential to profoundly expand access to vital medical care.

kp.k: Mobile access and professional augmentation remained prospective benefits
kp.d: The authors propose that mobile deployment could extend dermatological care outside clinics, broaden primary-care practice and augment specialist decisions. They link potential low-cost universal diagnostic access to a cited projection of 6.3 billion smartphone subscriptions by 2021. Earlier detection and improved access are proposed benefits, not clinical outcomes demonstrated by the study; adaptation to other image-based specialties is likewise conditional on sufficient training data.
qs: Outfitted with deep neural networks, mobile devices can potentially extend the reach of dermatologists outside of the clinic.
It is projected that 6.3 billion smartphone subscriptions will exist by the year 2021 (ref. 13) and can therefore potentially provide low-cost universal access to vital diagnostic care.

This fast, scalable method is deployable on mobile devices and holds the potential for substantial clinical impact, including broadening the scope of primary care practice and augmenting clinical decision-making for dermatology specialists.
This method is primarily constrained by data and can classify many visual conditions if sufficient training examples exist.
Deep learning is agnostic to the type of image data used and could be adapted to other specialties, including ophthalmology, otolaryngology, radiology and pathology.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Esteva and co-authors report dermatologist-comparable performance on specified image-classification tasks, rather than equivalence across the full practice of dermatology.
pts.d: In this 2017 cross-domain source, the authors claim that a single CNN matches tested dermatologists in distinguishing keratinocyte carcinomas from benign seborrheic keratoses and malignant melanomas from benign nevi, with melanoma tested using both ordinary photographs and dermoscopy. They also report outperforming the average dermatologist on these tests. Their claim concerns image-based classification, not replacement of clinicians or an entire diagnostic pathway.

pts.k: The authors predict potential expansion of diagnostic access, earlier detection and clinician augmentation through scalable, mobile AI.
pts.d: The authors describe mobile deployment as a potential means of extending dermatological care outside clinics and providing low-cost access. They suggest that practitioners and patients could track lesions and detect cancer earlier, while primary care practitioners could broaden their scope and dermatologists could receive decision support. These are prospective applications, not reported outcomes of a clinical deployment. They also propose adaptation to other image-based medical specialties.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The performance claim rests on training at scale and comparisons with board-certified dermatologists using held-out, biopsy-proven images.
pts.d: The authors describe a dataset of 129,450 clinical images covering 2,032 diseases, partitioned into 757 training classes, and transfer learning from approximately 1.28 million ImageNet images. Direct comparisons used 135 epidermal, 130 melanocytic photographic and 111 melanocytic dermoscopy images, assessed by 25, 22 and 21 dermatologists respectively. Dermatologists chose biopsy/treatment or reassurance. The CNN's threshold-swept sensitivity–specificity curves were compared with individual clinicians' operating points. AUC exceeded 0.91 for each comparison; this is not a reported percentage accuracy. Larger CNN-only tests comprised 707, 225 and 1,010 images respectively, with AUC changes below 0.03. The authors report no lesion overlap between test and training/validation data.

pts.k: Broader classification claims have qualified validation evidence; access and early-detection predictions are supported by feasibility arguments and background statistics rather than deployment results.
pts.d: Nine-fold cross-validation yielded 72.1 ± 0.9% accuracy for three broad disease classes and 55.4 ± 1.7% for nine classes, compared with 65.56% and 66.0%, and 53.3% and 55.0%, for two dermatologists on validation subsets. The authors explicitly call this evidence inconclusive because labels were not necessarily biopsy-confirmed. Their access argument cites a 2016 Ericsson projection of 6.3 billion smartphone subscriptions by 2021. Their early-detection rationale cites melanoma survival differences by stage. Neither improved patient outcomes, low-cost universal access nor effectiveness in other specialties is directly demonstrated in the reported study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The classification result is presented as achieved in 2017; clinical and access benefits remain conditional future possibilities without a deployment deadline.
pts.d: The only explicit future date is 2021 for the cited smartphone-subscription forecast, not a promised date for universal diagnostic care. The authors require further real-world clinical evaluation across the full range of lesions and acknowledge that clinical diagnosis uses context beyond isolated images. Tests used high-quality biopsy-proven repositories, excluded blurry or far-away test images, and restricted binary inference to lesions already known to be epidermal or melanocytic. Extension to additional visual conditions is conditional on sufficient training examples.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The anticipated beneficiaries are patients, primary care practitioners and dermatology specialists, with possible extensions to other medical specialties.
pts.d: Patients, including people outside clinic settings, are envisaged as gaining more accessible diagnostic care and opportunities for lesion tracking and earlier detection. Primary care practitioners could undertake a broader scope of care, and dermatologists could receive augmented decision support. Ophthalmology, otolaryngology, radiology and pathology are named as possible future application domains. The authors do not predict clinician job losses, staffing changes or legal-services impacts; the professional framing is principally augmentation and expanded reach.
